description: Width tiers for HASS Year 1 — ACARA v9. One entry per descriptor. K-strand descriptors use phenomena_contexts; S-strand descriptors use task_contexts.
subject: HASS

width_notes.minimum_width: For K-strand (Knowledge) descriptors: the narrowest set of phenomena or contexts that honestly satisfies the descriptor's command term — typically one family structure type, one place category, or one temporal comparison pair. For S-strand (Skills/Inquiry) descriptors: the narrowest task context in which the skill is applied — one source type, one topic, one presentation format.
width_notes.typical_width: For K-strand descriptors: engagement across the range of examples indicated by elaborations — multiple family types, place feature categories, or comparison cases. For S-strand descriptors: the skill applied across two or more task types or contexts representative of the elaboration range.
width_notes.wider: Enrichment directions that add new phenomena, cultural contexts, or task contexts — not harder versions of the same. First Nations elaborations always appear in wider where present in ACARA source material.
width_notes.elaborations: ACARA elaborations used as source data to ground typical_width and identify wider directions. First Nations elaborations consistently placed in wider.

AC9HS1K01.minimum_width: Identify one or two different family structures and describe how roles within them differ from each other.
AC9HS1K01.typical_width: Compare a range of family structures (nuclear, extended, single-parent, blended, grandparent families, kinship groups) and describe how roles of parents, children and extended family members have changed or stayed the same over time.
wider: Examine how family roles and structures in First Nations Australian kinship systems — including extended kin obligations and community responsibilities — differ from Western nuclear family norms
Compare family structures from two or more different cultural backgrounds represented in the class, identifying similarities and differences in how roles are defined
elaborations: identifying the similarities and differences of a range of family structures; for example, nuclear families, one-child families, large families, single-parent families, extended families, blended or step families, adoptive and foster parent families and grandparent families, and kinship groups
comparing families in the present with those from the recent past, for example, the size of families across the generations
examining the roles of family members over time, such as roles of parents, children and extended family members, and comparing these with family roles today

AC9HS1K02.minimum_width: Identify one aspect of daily life that has changed between their childhood and a parent's or grandparent's childhood.
AC9HS1K02.typical_width: Compare multiple aspects of daily life — homes, school, leisure, shopping, religious and cultural practices — across generations using oral histories, photographs and other sources; identify examples of continuity alongside change.
wider: Investigate traditional toys and games used by First Nations Australian children — for example, Arrernte string games for story transmission — and compare their purposes with contemporary children's play
Examine how diverse cultural and religious practices have shaped different families' daily life traditions, using classmates' family experiences as sources
elaborations: comparing and commenting on photographs and oral histories to find out how daily lives have changed and remained the same over time; for example, talking to parents, grandparents and other elders
comparing what has changed in daily life over time; for example, homes, family traditions, diverse religious and cultural practices, leisure, school life, rules, and shopping/consumer habits
examining the traditional toys used by First Nations Australian children to play and learn; for example, Arrernte children learn to play string games so they can remember stories they have been told

identifying similarities and differences in classroom equipment, learning activities, school playgrounds and playground games through observations of provided artefacts and photos, and asking questions of adults from different generations

AC9HS1K03.minimum_width: Identify at least one natural and one constructed feature of their local place and locate them on a simple map.
AC9HS1K03.typical_width: Identify and describe natural, managed and constructed features of local places; locate them on a map; describe the weather of their place using simple terms and compare it with another place.
wider: Explore Dreaming and Creation stories of First Nations Australians that describe and explain the natural features of a specific place, comparing this way of knowing a place with map-based geographical description
Describe and compare the seasonal weather patterns of their local place with a contrasting Australian place, explaining how weather shapes daily life in each
elaborations: identifying natural features (for example, hills, rivers, native vegetation and weather), managed features (for example, farms, parks and gardens) and constructed features (for example, roads and buildings) and locating them on a map
listening to and viewing Dreaming and Creation stories of First Nations Australians that identify the natural features of a place
listing the different types of buildings in their local area; for example, houses, shops, offices, factories, religious buildings and farm buildings

describing the daily and seasonal weather of their place using simple terms such as "rainy", "hot", "cold", "windy" and "cloudy", and comparing it with the weather of other places that they know or are aware of; for example, "It was windy at the beach but not at my house", "It is colder on the mountain", "It is rainy in the winter", "It is hot in the summer"

explaining to classmates where places are and the directions to be followed when moving from one place to another, with the use of appropriate terms for direction and location; for example, terms such as "beside", "forward", "up", "down", "by", "near", "further", "close to", "before", "after", "here", "there", "at"

AC9HS1K04.minimum_width: Describe one way that a local place has changed and identify who cares for it.
AC9HS1K04.typical_width: Describe multiple ways that local places change — through seasons, erosion, new buildings, revegetation — and identify different groups, including community organisations, who care for those places and why.
wider: Investigate examples of how First Nations Australians manage and care for specific places — for example, cultural burning practices, land management systems — and compare with contemporary local government approaches
Explore how recycling and waste reduction systems in the local area connect to broader environmental care responsibilities, identifying student roles within those systems
elaborations: observing changes in natural, managed and constructed features in their place; for example, recent erosion, revegetated areas, planted crops or new buildings
identifying which resources they can recycle, reduce, re-use or none of these, and what local spaces and systems support these activities; for example, rules, signs, waste collection truck routes

describing how local places change due to changing weather and seasons, and how we can care for places because of those changes; for example, not walking in muddy areas during wet weather, and watering plants in dry weather

describing local features that people look after, finding out why and how these features need to be cared for, and who provides this care; for example, bushland, wetlands, a park or a heritage building
investigating examples of how First Nations Australians manage and care for places

AC9HS1S01.minimum_width: Develop at least one question about an object, person or place using a 'where', 'what', 'how' or 'why' stem.
AC9HS1S01.typical_width: Develop questions across multiple inquiry contexts — families, places, the past and present — using a range of question stems; prepare questions for interviews with older people about their lives and places they value.
wider: Generate questions before, during and after engaging with a source (stories, maps, observations) rather than only at the start of an inquiry
Develop questions that probe perspectives — for example, 'Why might this place be important to someone different from me?' — extending beyond factual 'what' questions
elaborations: posing questions with the stems "where", "what", "how" and "why" about families and places when provided with everyday objects and other sources, such as photos, found objects, maps and observation sketches
asking questions before, during and after listening to stories about people and places, and about their past and present
preparing questions for parents and members of older generations about how and where they lived in the past, and the places they value

AC9HS1S02.minimum_width: Collect information from one provided source type (for example, a story or photograph) and record it in a simple format (table, drawing or map label).
AC9HS1S02.typical_width: Collect, sort and record information from multiple source types including stories, aerial photographs, oral histories and observations; create pictorial tables, peg timelines and labelled maps to organise the information.
wider: Collect information about places across multiple representation types — field observation, aerial photograph, drawn map — and compare what each type of source reveals
Explore stories from First Nations Australian oral and visual traditions (myths, Dreaming stories, story maps) as source material for recording information about places and the past
elaborations: exploring stories from the past and present about people and families (for example, fiction books, letters, diaries, songs) and about places (for example, myths, Dreaming and Creation stories, fiction, story maps, films)

gathering evidence of features in a local place; for example, using observations, online aerial photographs and sketches, and noting how they change, such as by comparing current observations of a place with photographs of it taken in the past, or recording observations of weather and seasons
developing a pictorial table to categorise information; for example, matching clothes with seasons, activities with the weather, features with places, places with the work done there
creating a peg timeline in which labelled, drawn or photographic representations of events or objects from different generations are pegged onto string in the correct sequence

recording data about the locations of places and their features on maps and/or plans; for example, labelling the location of their home on a map of the local area, using a provided plan of their classroom and labelling its activity spaces

AC9HS1S03.minimum_width: Use information from one source to answer a 'when', 'where', 'what', 'how' or 'why' question about a familiar topic.
AC9HS1S03.typical_width: Interpret information from multiple source types (photographs, satellite images, rock art, stories) to answer questions about the past and present; use comparative language to describe family life over time and features of places.
wider: Explore traditional and contemporary First Nations Australian stories about places and the past, interpreting how these sources represent change over time differently from photographs or written records
Interpret the same place or event using two different source types and identify what each reveals that the other does not — for example, a photograph versus a Dreaming story about the same location
elaborations: using information gained from sources, such as stories, photographs, fieldwork observations, satellite images and rock art, to answer "when", "where", "what", "how" and "why" questions

identifying similarities and differences between activities over time by comparing objects of the past with those currently used; for example, comparing toys, games, clothes, phones, cooking utensils, tools, homework books

using comparative language when describing family life over time and/or comparing features of places, such as "smaller/bigger than", "closer/further", "not as big as", "younger/older than", "more rainy days", "fewer/less", "hotter/colder", "sunnier/windier than"
exploring traditional and contemporary First Nations Australian stories about places and the past, and how places have changed

categorising objects, drawings or images by their features and explaining the reason for their categorisation; for example, categorising the features of a local place into natural (such as a native forest), constructed (such as a street of houses) and managed (such as a windbreak of trees)

AC9HS1S04.minimum_width: Share a personal preference about one aspect of their world (for example, a favourite place or activity) and give a reason.
AC9HS1S04.typical_width: Discuss perspectives by comparing students' daily lives with those of older generations; share and explain personal preferences about weather, places, celebrations and objects, identifying what they would or would not want to experience from the past.
wider: Compare perspectives across cultural backgrounds — for example, exploring how different students' families celebrate the same season or event differently, and what this reveals about perspective
Examine how a grandparent's or elder's perspective on a changed place differs from their own, identifying what shapes each perspective
elaborations: comparing students' daily lives with those of their parents, grandparents, elders or a familiar older person and identifying which aspects of the past they would or would not want to experience
sharing personal preferences about their world (for example, their favourite weather, activities, places, celebrations, objects from the past) and explaining why they are favoured

AC9HS1S05.minimum_width: Use collected information to draw one conclusion about continuity or change — for example, how a family role or technology has changed.
AC9HS1S05.typical_width: Use collected information to draw conclusions about continuity and change over time and how places change with seasons; describe a special place and propose an action to care for it.
wider: Propose actions for how a local place could be improved and explain how the proposal addresses a specific identified problem — moving beyond description to reasoned recommendation
Imagine how a local feature might change in the future and develop two or more alternative scenarios (one probable, one preferred), explaining the difference
elaborations: using collected information (for example, from stories told by parents, grandparents, elders or familiar older people; from comparison of objects; from geographic pictures) to make conclusions about continuity and change over time (for example, how family roles, occupations and/or technologies have changed or remained the same) and how places change (for example, because of the seasons)

describing features of a space or place that is important to them and explaining what they could do to care for it; for example, a chicken coop, a play area, their bedroom, the reading corner, the beach
imagining how a local feature or place might change in the future and proposing action they could take to improve a place or influence a positive future

AC9HS1S06.minimum_width: Retell one story about life in the past using pictures or spoken words; use at least one time term correctly.
AC9HS1S06.typical_width: Develop narratives about the past using spoken words, pictures or role-play; share observations about places; use time terms (then, now, past, present, future, generations) correctly and consistently.
wider: Present a narrative that combines both time terms and place description — situating a story both in when and where it happened
Use role-play or dramatisation as a mode of narrative, applying time terms within character perspectives from different generations
elaborations: retelling stories about life in the past through spoken narratives and the use of pictures, role-plays or photographs
using terms to denote the sequence of time; for example, "then", "now", "yesterday", "today", "past", "present", "later on", "before I was born", "in the future", "generations"
